cannot_tell.text: The central line rests on 9 US transit upzonings, each smaller than a statewide law. Whether the extra homes on upzoned lots are new or moved from farther across town could not be measured; building next door did not fall.
cannot_tell.title: Whether Wisconsin will behave like the 9 reform cities

cannot_tell.text: We tested 12 local traits (home values, incomes, rents, lot sizes, existing density, distance to downtown and others) and all 66 pairs of them, then 91 census variables (housing, incomes, commuting, car ownership and more), with 8 prediction methods including random and causal forests, predicting each of 8 cities from the others. None reliably predicts where upzoning added more homes, so the scenarios stay wide (docs/tod/TRAITS_RESULTS.md, docs/tod/ALLVARS_RESULTS.md).
cannot_tell.title: Why the response differs from place to place

cannot_tell.text: The studies measured their effects three or more years after each reform. The model places that effect inside 2027–2031, the law's first five years. Much of a real law's effect may come after 2031, so the yearly path is the least certain part of these numbers.

groups.label: What-ifs that change the law's addition

rows.label: Smoother final year
rows.text: Year 2031 set to the average of 2029–2031 instead of the measured New York drop. Changes timing only; the five-year totals stay the same.

rows.label: Central line at the low and high ends of its range
rows.text: The upzoned-share trend refitted 9 times, each time leaving one reform city out.

rows.label: Little-or-no line at the low and high ends of its range
rows.text: The station-area model refitted 16 times, each time leaving one place out. The low end is below zero: no floor is set where the evidence does not set one.

rows.label: Former little line: Los Angeles's transit program
rows.text: Los Angeles's Transit Oriented Communities program (2017) added 0.04 percentage points to the city's housing growth over six years (per upzoned home). It required affordable homes, which the modelled law does not.

rows.label: Little-or-no line if affordability rules held the broad programs back
rows.text: The station-area model with a trait for programs that required affordable homes (Los Angeles, San Diego, Chicago 2022). The trait did not improve predictions for hidden places, so it is not in the main line.

rows.label: Former typical line: the average loosening reform
rows.text: Stacy and others (2023): about +0.8% more addresses after a loosening reform in 1,136 US cities. Most of those reforms were about accessory dwellings and lot sizes, not transit upzonings.

rows.label: Lot model, rule set in advance (pre-registered)
rows.text: Every reform city's average rise in the upzoned lots' share of new homes (+4.0 points), applied to Wisconsin. The central line's drift rule was found after seeing results (post hoc); this is the rule logged beforehand.

rows.label: Each study's effect as published
rows.text: Not adjusted for how much of each city the reform covered (Los Angeles about 61% of homes, Auckland 75.2% of residential land).

rows.label: Strong response timed like New York
rows.text: The strong response spread over the years like the New York rezonings instead of Auckland's own pattern. Same five-year total.

groups.label: What-ifs that change where the homes land (and, for the stop rules, how many homes are near stops)

rows.label: Only Milwaukee and Madison get homes
rows.text: The suburbs, whose zoning rules were not entered into the model, get none of the extra homes.

rows.label: Suburbs' estimated room not scaled down
rows.text: The suburbs' room for new homes is estimated from existing buildings and not scaled by 0.719.

rows.label: Only rail and rapid transit stations count
rows.text: Buses every 15 minutes do not qualify. Fewer homes are near stops, so fewer homes are expected near stops both with and without the law.

rows.label: Buses every 20 minutes count too
rows.text: Adds 20-minute bus routes within ¼ mile, including Eau Claire's.

rows.label: All 15-minute stops count within ½ mile
rows.text: Bus stops get the same ½ mile as stations.

groups.label: What-ifs that change current law only

rows.label: Milwaukee's apartments as the Census published them
rows.text: The Census permit file misses most of Milwaukee's apartments; the main case uses the city's property file instead.

trace.part: Bus and train stops, and how often buses come
trace.text: Stop locations from the federal National Transit Map; frequencies from each agency's own schedule file or, for Madison, its published route descriptions.
2020 census homes in blocks whose centre lies within the distance: 313,564 homes in the main case.
Each place's expected new homes under current law (Census building permits, 2023–2025 average, with Milwaukee's apartments counted from its property records), times its share of homes near stops.

The little-or-no line comes from our station-area model: building near 16 US places' reform stations compared with similar stations without reform, every lot within a mile, tested by hiding one place at a time; it beat simple rules only within a quarter mile, and broad upzonings near every station gained about nothing (docs/tod/STATION_AREA_PLAN.md; 1,275 large projects checked by hand, removing hotel rooms, storage units and beds counted as homes). The strong line comes from a published study of a whole city's net gain in homes after upzoning (Auckland), divided by its coverage. The central line comes from the trend in upzoned lots' share of new homes in 9 US transit upzonings, from our lot data (docs/tod/MODEL_MENU_RESULTS.md).

trace.part: That those results carry over to Wisconsin
trace.text: No Wisconsin outcome has tested the sizing. Milwaukee's and Madison's shares of homes near stops (68% and 63%) are close to Los Angeles's 61% coverage. A check near Milwaukee's streetcar, with no rezoning, found building rose about as much as in a typical reform city, so quarter-mile gains of that size can happen without zoning changes.
The little response and the central line follow the build-up measured after the New York rezonings; the strong response follows Auckland's own yearly pattern.

trace.part: Where homes land in Milwaukee and Madison
trace.text: From the two cities' zoning codes, entered rule by rule: the extra floor area the law allows on each piece of land. These two cities get 41% of the central line's homes.

trace.part: Where homes land in the suburbs
trace.text: Their zoning rules were not entered, so the room for new homes is estimated from existing buildings and scaled by 0.719, the ratio measured in Milwaukee and Madison. The suburbs get 59% of the central line's homes.
Each place's numbers are split across districts in proportion to where its detached houses are (the same split the ADU screens use), not by homes near stops.
